figures.label: Figure 1
figures.caption: Figure 1: The Transformer - model architecture.
figures.reading:
1. **Figure Type:** Architecture diagram.

2. **Content:** The diagram shows the Transformer model architecture, consisting of an encoder (left) and a decoder (right). The flow is bottom-up. The encoder takes "Inputs" through an "Input Embedding" layer, adds "Positional Encoding", and passes them into a stack of N identical layers. Each encoder layer contains a "Multi-Head Attention" block followed by an "Add & Norm" step, then a "Feed Forward" block followed by another "Add & Norm" step. The decoder takes "Outputs (shifted right)" through an "Output Embedding", adds "Positional Encoding", and passes them into a stack of N identical layers. Each decoder layer contains a "Masked Multi-Head Attention" block ("Add & Norm"), a "Multi-Head Attention" block ("Add & Norm") which receives input from the encoder, and a "Feed Forward" block ("Add & Norm"). The final output goes through a "Linear" layer and a "Softmax" layer to produce "Output Probabilities".

3. **Reported Numbers:**
*   **Nx** (next to the encoder block)
*   **Nx** (next to the decoder block)

figures.label: Figure 2
figures.caption: Figure 2: (left) Scaled Dot-Product Attention. (right) Multi-Head Attention consists of several attention layers running in parallel.
figures.reading:
This is an architecture diagram. It depicts two related computational structures: Scaled Dot-Product Attention (left) and Multi-Head Attention (right).

The left diagram shows a flow from bottom to top: inputs Q, K, and V enter a MatMul block, followed by Scale, an optional Mask (opt.), SoftMax, and a final MatMul that also takes V as input.

The right diagram shows a parallel structure where V, K, and Q each pass through separate Linear layers into h parallel Scaled Dot-Product Attention blocks. Their outputs are concatenated (Concat) and passed through a final Linear layer.

There are no reported numerical values in the figure.

figures.label: Table 1
figures.caption: Table 1: Maximum path lengths, per-layer complexity and minimum number of sequential operations for different layer types. n is the sequence length, d is the representation dimension, k is the kernel size of convolutions and r the size of the neighborhood in restricted self-attention.
figures.reading:
This is a results table. It compares four layer types (Self-Attention, Recurrent, Convolutional, Self-Attention (restricted)) across three columns: Complexity per Layer, Sequential Operations, and Maximum Path Length.

The reported values are:
*   **Self-Attention:** $O(n^2 \cdot d)$, $O(1)$, $O(1)$
*   **Recurrent:** $O(n \cdot d^2)$, $O(n)$, $O(n)$
*   **Convolutional:** $O(k \cdot n \cdot d^2)$, $O(1)$, $O(\log_k(n))$
*   **Self-Attention (restricted):** $O(r \cdot n \cdot d)$, $O(1)$, $O(n/r)$

figures.label: Table 2
figures.caption: Table 2: The Transformer achieves better BLEU scores than previous state-of-the-art models on the English-to-German and English-to-French newstest2014 tests at a fraction of the training cost.
figures.reading:
This is a results table. It compares various machine translation models across four columns: BLEU scores for English-to-German (EN-DE) and English-to-French (EN-FR), and Training Cost in FLOPs for both tasks.

The reported numbers are:
*   **ByteNet [18]:** EN-DE: 23.75; EN-FR: 39.2; EN-FR Cost: 1.0 · 10^20
*   **Deep-Att + PosUnk [39]:** EN-FR: 39.2; EN-FR Cost: 1.0 · 10^20
*   **GNMT + RL [38]:** EN-DE: 24.6; EN-FR: 39.92; EN-DE Cost: 2.3 · 10^19; EN-FR Cost: 1.4 · 10^20
*   **ConvS2S [9]:** EN-DE: 25.16; EN-FR: 40.46; EN-DE Cost: 9.6 · 10^18; EN-FR Cost: 1.5 · 10^20
*   **MoE [32]:** EN-DE: 26.03; EN-FR: 40.56; EN-DE Cost: 2.0 · 10^19; EN-FR Cost: 1.2 · 10^20
*   **Deep-Att + PosUnk Ensemble [39]:** EN-FR: 40.4; EN-FR Cost: 8.0 · 10^20
*   **GNMT + RL Ensemble [38]:** EN-DE: 26.30; EN-FR: 41.16; EN-DE Cost: 1.8 · 10^20; EN-FR Cost: 1.1 · 10^21
*   **ConvS2S Ensemble [9]:** EN-DE: 26.36; EN-FR: 41.29; EN-DE Cost: 7.7 · 10^19; EN-FR Cost: 1.2 · 10^21
*   **Transformer (base model):** EN-DE: 27.3; EN-FR: 38.1; EN-DE Cost: 3.3 · 10^18
*   **Transformer (big):** EN-DE: 28.4; EN-FR: 41.8; EN-DE Cost: 2.3 · 10^19

figures.label: Table 3
figures.caption: Table 3: Variations on the Transformer architecture. Unlisted values are identical to those of the base model. All metrics are on the English-to-German translation development set, newstest2013. Listed perplexities are per-wordpiece, according to our byte-pair encoding, and should not be compared to per-word perplexities.

figures.label: Figure 3
figures.caption: Figure 3: An example of the attention mechanism following long-distance dependencies in the encoder self-attention in layer 5 of 6. Many of the attention heads attend to a distant dependency of the verb ‘making’, completing the phrase ‘making...more difficult’. Attentions here shown only for the word ‘making’. Different colors represent different heads. Best viewed in color.
figures.reading:
This is an attention visualization plot. It displays the attention weights for the word "making" in a sentence, with the x-axis representing the sequence of tokens and the y-axis representing different attention heads (indicated by color). The lines show the flow of attention from the token "making" to other tokens in the sequence.

The tokens on the x-axis are: "it", "is", "in", "this", "spirit", "that", "a", "majority", "of", "American", "governments", "have", "passed", "new", "laws", "since", "2009", "making", "the", "registration", "or", "voting", "process", "more", "difficult", ".", "<EOS>", followed by several "<pad>" tokens.

There are no specific numerical values legibly printed within the figure itself; it uses color intensity and line thickness to represent attention weights.

figures.label: Figure 4
figures.caption: Figure 4: Two attention heads, also in layer 5 of 6, apparently involved in anaphora resolution. Top: Full attentions for head 5. Bottom: Isolated attentions from just the word ‘its’ for attention heads 5 and 6. Note that the attentions are very sharp for this word.
figures.reading:
This is an architecture diagram (specifically, an attention visualization). It displays attention weights between words in a sentence. The components are two horizontal rows of text tokens (the source and target sequences), with lines connecting them to represent the direction and strength of attention flow from the bottom row to the top row.

The figure is divided into two parts:
- **Top:** Shows full attentions for head 5.
- **Bottom:** Shows isolated attentions for the word "its" for heads 5 and 6.

The text tokens in the sequence are:
The, Law, will, never, be, perfect, ., but, its, application, should, be, just, ., this, is, what, we, are, missing, ., in, my, opinion, ., <EOS>, <pad>

There are no numerical values reported or legible in the figure itself; the information is conveyed through the visual density and color of the connecting lines.

figures.label: Figure 5
figures.caption: Figure 5: Many of the attention heads exhibit behaviour that seems related to the structure of the sentence. We give two such examples above, from two different heads from the encoder self-attention at layer 5 of 6. The heads clearly learned to perform different tasks.
figures.reading: This is a plot showing two attention weight visualizations, one in green and one in red. The horizontal axes represent the sequence of tokens: "The", "Law", "will", "never", "be", "perfect", ",", "but", "its", "application", "should", "be", "just", ".", "this", "is", "what", "we", "are", "missing", ",", "in", "my", "opinion", ".", "<EOS>", "<pad>". The vertical axis represents the attention weights from each token to all other tokens. The green plot shows strong attention from the token "Law" to itself and from "missing" to itself, as well as from "opinion" to itself. The red plot shows strong attention from "The", "be", "perfect", "application", "just", "what", "missing", and "<pad>" to themselves. No numerical values are legible on the figure.
